stages.name: Trade restrictions: revenue
stages.title: Trade restrictions: revenue
stages.sub: See why governments sometimes restrict trade simply to collect money.

steps.q: A government adds a charge on every packet of imported cigarettes entering the country, on top of the selling price. What kind of charge does this look like?
steps.right: A tax added onto a good
steps.hint: Think about what an indirect tax on a good looks like, just applied at the border instead of in the shop.

steps.q: People keep buying the imported cigarettes anyway, month after month, despite the extra charge. What happens to the amount coming into the country over time?
steps.right: It keeps coming in fairly steadily
steps.hint: If demand for the good barely changes, do imports dry up or carry on?

steps.q: Hospitals, schools and roads all need to be paid for, year after year. Does the government's need for money ever disappear?
steps.right: No, it needs a constant flow of funds
steps.wrong: Yes, once budgets are set the need ends
steps.hint: Think about whether public services stop needing funding once one year's bills are paid.

steps.q: Every packet that keeps entering still has that extra charge collected on it by customs, feeding into the funds needed for public spending. What does this steady stream of charges become for the government?
steps.wrong: A cost it has to cover
steps.hint: Who is receiving the money collected on each packet, and does it stop?
